name: Teton Dam, Idaho, USA (1976)

sources.citation: Bureau of Reclamation, Teton Dam History
ASDSO Dam Failures and Lessons Learned, Teton Dam (Idaho, 1976) case study
Simulating the 1976 Teton Dam Failure using Geoclaw and HEC-RAS and comparing with Historical Observations, arXiv:2206.00766
USGS, Summary of Significant Floods in the US, PR, and the VI, 1970-1989 (2008), via usdeadlyevents.com compilation

sourced.crestElev: structural height 305 ft ≈ 93 m (ASDSO case study)
sourced.initialWL: 82 m water surface elevation above riverbed at time of failure — reservoir had not yet reached full pool (arXiv:2206.00766)
sourced.volumeM3: 2.89e8 m3 = 234,260 acre-ft, reservoir volume at time of failure, below the 3.55e8 m3 design capacity (arXiv:2206.00766, citing Reclamation 2006)
sourced.collapseRatio: Derived, not directly reported: multiple independent sources (NWS Heritage; Alabama Weather Network) report the internal erosion hole reached ~25 ft (7.6 m) diameter shortly before the final catastrophic collapse. Taking that as the pipe diameter (2R) at collapse and cover = crestElev - pipeInvert = 89 m (pipeInvert itself still a placeholder, see below), collapseRatio = 2R/cover = 7.6/89 ≈ 0.086. This is an approximation, not an exact match of model quantities -- the reported '25 ft hole' is the visible surface/whirlpool expression, which is not guaranteed to equal the model's idealized internal pipe throat diameter exactly. Still a large, well-sourced improvement over the previous default (0.55), which allowed the simulated pipe to reach ~49 m diameter before collapsing -- about 6x larger than what was actually observed.

sourcingCaveat: Teton's real failure mechanism was seepage through open joints in fissured rhyolite foundation rock near the right abutment, eroding the adjacent embankment core at the rock/fill contact -- not a simple pipe forming through the middle of a homogeneous embankment. This engine's 'piping' mode models the latter (idealized circular conduit through the fill). Both erosionIndexI and pipeInvert remain unsourced placeholders as a result: literature consistently describes the core material (non-plastic windblown loess) as among the most erodible soil classes in the Wan & Fell (2004) Erosion Rate Index scheme, which if anything argues for a LOWER erosionIndexI than the current default 3.2 (more erodible), not a higher one -- so 'fixing' erosionIndexI alone would not resolve the Qpeak/timing overestimate and could make it worse. No numeric erosionIndexI/tauC specific to Teton was found via search; the Bureau of Reclamation's original forensic investigation almost certainly has lab-tested values and would be the authoritative source if available.
unsourcedFieldsNote: These use DEFAULT_INPUTS' typical zoned-earthfill values. The actual Bureau of Reclamation forensic investigation almost certainly has real erodibility/pipe-geometry data for this dam; replace these before treating this case as a rigorous validation rather than a plausibility check.

peakDischargeM3s.note: USGS estimate of 2.3 million ft3/s converted to SI (≈65,130 m3/s); some sources round to ~2.3–2.4 million cfs.

breachFormationHours.note: Reclamation analysis: significant internal destruction occurred over ~1 hour, 11:00–11:57 on 1976-06-05 (arXiv:2206.00766, citing Solava & Delatte 2003 / Reclamation 1976). Full reservoir drained (173,000 acre-ft) in 2h23m, a separate, longer figure — use breachFormationHours for the erosion/enlargement phase, not total drawdown.
